questions.q: In data parallelism, what does each GPU hold and process?
options: A different slice of the model's layers, processing the full dataset
A single shared copy of the model that all GPUs write to simultaneously without synchronization
No model at all — GPUs only store gradients computed elsewhere
A complete copy of the entire model, each processing a different shard of the training data
questions.explain: Data parallelism replicates the full model on every GPU. Each replica trains independently on its own slice of the data, and the replicas are kept in sync through gradient synchronization.

questions.q: What does the AllReduce operation accomplish in data-parallel training?
options: It deletes gradients from all but one GPU to save memory
It splits the model into smaller pieces across GPUs
It sums/averages each GPU's locally computed gradients across all GPUs and broadcasts the result back, so every replica applies the identical update
It compresses the training dataset before each epoch
questions.explain: Without reconciling gradients, each GPU's model replica would drift apart after independent updates. AllReduce combines gradients across all GPUs and returns the same result to each, keeping replicas identical.

questions.q: Why does model parallelism exist as a separate strategy from data parallelism?
options: Model parallelism is simply a faster version of data parallelism with no functional difference
Model parallelism addresses the case where the model itself doesn't fit on a single GPU, so replicating the whole model everywhere isn't possible in the first place
Model parallelism is only used for inference, never for training
Model parallelism replaces the need for any GPU-to-GPU communication entirely
questions.explain: Data parallelism assumes the model already fits on one GPU. When it doesn't — no matter how small the batch — replication isn't an option, so the model itself has to be split across GPUs instead.

questions.q: What distinguishes tensor parallelism from pipeline parallelism?
options: Tensor parallelism splits individual layers' weight matrices across GPUs with every GPU participating in every layer; pipeline parallelism splits the model by groups of layers, with data flowing stage by stage
Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism are two names for the exact same technique
Pipeline parallelism splits individual weight matrices, while tensor parallelism assigns whole layers to different GPUs
Tensor parallelism is used only for data loading, never for model computation
questions.explain: Tensor parallelism cuts within a layer — e.g. splitting a weight matrix's columns across GPUs that all compute part of the same layer. Pipeline parallelism cuts across layers, assigning groups of layers to different GPUs as pipeline stages.

questions.q: Why do production-scale training clusters typically combine data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism together ("3D parallelism") rather than using just one?
options: Because regulations require at least three forms of parallelism for any model above a certain size
Because each form of parallelism solves a different piece of the memory-and-time problem, and combining them lets training scale across both GPUs within a machine and across many machines
Because using only one form of parallelism is technically impossible on modern hardware
Because 3D parallelism eliminates the need for GPUs entirely by shifting compute to CPUs
questions.explain: Tensor parallelism handles fast intra-layer splits best suited to NVLink-connected GPUs; pipeline parallelism tolerates slower inter-machine links; data parallelism replicates the resulting shard across groups of machines. Together they address memory limits and training time at the largest scales.
